items.question: Across 6 years of high-frequency data at Falling Creek Reservoir, did variability in ice-cover duration meaningfully change annual whole-reservoir metabolism (NEP)? How did winter rates compare to summer, and why did this contrast with higher-latitude lakes?
items.answer:
Variability in ice-cover duration over six years at Falling Creek Reservoir did not meaningfully change annual whole-reservoir metabolism (NEP). Despite substantial year-to-year differences in ice duration (ranging from 0 to 35 days), annual rates of gross primary production, respiration, and NEP remained consistent across all years studied [2][4][5]. This stability is attributed to the reservoir’s short and variable winter periods, which meant that winter data had only a limited effect on annual metabolism estimates—unlike higher-latitude lakes, where longer ice cover can significantly impact annual metabolic budgets [3].

Winter NEP rates at Falling Creek Reservoir were similar to those observed in other seasons, indicating that the brief winter periods did not drive major seasonal contrasts in whole-lake metabolism [4]. This contrasts with higher-latitude lakes, where extended ice cover typically leads to lower metabolic rates in winter and a stronger seasonal signal. The difference arises because Falling Creek Reservoir’s short ice duration limits the influence of winter on annual metabolism, whereas in higher-latitude systems, prolonged ice cover can suppress metabolic activity for a much larger portion of the year [3][4].

Water chemistry, rather than ice duration, explained most of the observed variability in daily gross primary production, but not in respiration or NEP, further supporting the limited role of ice-cover variability in shaping annual metabolism at this site [5].

Confidence: High, as these findings are supported by six years of high-frequency sensor data and consistent annual estimates reported in the literature [2][4][5].
contexts: A six-year study of Falling Creek Reservoir, a eutrophic lake in Virginia, examined carbon cycling and lake metabolism under variable ice cover using high-frequency oxygen and environmental data. Results showed consistent annual rates of gross primary production, respiration, and net ecosystem production despite differences in ice duration, with winter metabolism comparable to other seasons. Nutrient concentrations influenced daily primary production variability, while respiration and net ecosystem production showed less sensitivity to environmental drivers. The study provides valuable insights into carbon dynamics in lakes experiencing changing ice cover.

A six-year study of a eutrophic reservoir with variable ice cover revealed consistent annual lake metabolism rates—gross primary production (GPP), respiration (R), and net ecosystem production (NEP)—despite differences in ice duration, with winter metabolism rates comparable to other seasons. Water chemistry, particularly nutrient concentrations, influenced daily GPP variability but had limited effect on R or NEP, and no strong environmental drivers for R or NEP were identified. The research also highlighted greater inter-annual variability in NEP compared to GPP and R, and emphasized the importance of seasonal classifications and thermal stratification in understanding metabolic dynamics in reservoirs.

Author Contri butions:

Abstract Temperate reservoirs and lakes worldwide are experiencing decreases in ice cover, which will likely alter the net balance of gross primary production (GPP) and respiration (R) in these ecosystems. However, most metabolism studies to date have focused on summer dynamics, thereby excluding winter dynamics from annual metabolism budgets. To address this gap, we analyzed 6 years of year-round high-frequency dissolved oxygen data to estimate daily rates of net ecosystem production (NEP), GPP, and R in a eutrophic, dimictic reservoir that has intermittent ice cover. Over 6 years, the reservoir exhibited slight heterotrophy during both summer and winter. We found winter and summer metabolism rates to be similar: summer NEP had a median rate of 0.06 mg O 2 L 1 day 1 (range: 15.86 to 3.20 mg O 2 L 1 day 1 ), while median winter NEP was 0.02 mg O 2 L 1 day 1 (range: 8.19 to 0.53 mg O 2 L 1 day 1 ). Despite large differences in the duration of ice cover among years, there were minimal differences in NEP among winters. Overall, the inclusion of winter data had a limited effect on annual metabolism estimates in a eutrophic reservoir, likely due to short winter periods in this reservoir (ice durations 0-35 days), relative to higher-latitude lakes. Our work reveals a smaller difference between winter and summer NEP than in lakes with continuous ice cover. Ultimately, our work underscores the importance of studying full-year metabolism dynamics in a range of aquatic ecosystems to help anticipate the effects of declining ice cover across lakes worldwide.

Journal of Geophysical Research: Biogeosciences

4. Discussion

These PMs were run inside the FLARE framework to generate a multi-model ensemble (MME) from the output (Figure 1), hereafter referred to as the PM MME forecast. To answer questions 2 and 3, two baseline models were also included to produce the full MME forecast (full MME, hereafter), which consisted of five individual models ( n = 3 PMs and n = 2 baseline models). Finally, these forecasts are evaluated using the in-situ water temperature observations (Figure 1) via a suite of metrics, described below.

2.2. Site Description and Data Collection

We generated water temperature forecasts for Falling Creek Reservoir (FCR), a eutrophic reservoir located in Vinton, Virginia, USA (37.30°N, 79.84°W). FCR is managed by the Western Virginia Water Authority as a drinking water source. The reservoir has a mean depth of 4 m and a maximum depth of 9.3 m, with a surface area of 0.12 km 2 (Carey et al., 2022 a). A dimictic system, FCR generally stratifies from May to October and has intermittent ice-cover from December to March (Carey & Breef-Pilz, 2023). The reservoir has one primary inflow and water level is maintained to be generally constant over time.

USA

Keywords: Mixing, Bubble plume, Hydrodynamic model, Destratification, Water quality

Abstract. Artificial mixing with bubble-plume devices is often used to deal with water quality problems in reservoirs, such as algal bloom and hypoxia. In general, the mixing results in an increase of dissolved oxygen in the water, as well as an increase in temperature in the deeper layers of the water body but a decrease in temperature in the upper layers. Underst anding the heat and oxygen transfer mechanisms will help to optimise the design and operation of the devices.

This study focuses on Falling Creek Reservoir (FCR), which is a shallow, eutrophic drinking water reservoir managed by the Western Virginia Water Authority, Virginia, USA. FCR is equipped with a bubble-plume epilimnetic mixer (EM) to cope with occasional algal blooms during the stratified periods. We adopt a validated three-dimensional hydrodynamic model Si 3 D to visualise and analyse the mixing per formance of the EM in FCR. It is found that the mixing with the EM placed in the deep region of FCR has a significant impact on the water temperature throughout the reservoir. The mixing reduces thermal stability, increases the metalimnetic temperature, and deepens the thermocline. Tracers are used in the model to further quantify the mixing per formance of the EM.

The study at Falling Creek Reservoir (FCR) utilized high-frequency temperature data collected from multiple depths between 2019 and 2023 to analyze lake temperature dynamics. Two simple empirical baseline models—a persistence model assuming no change over the forecast horizon and a day-of-year model based on historical daily means—were employed to forecast water temperatures. Observations revealed typical seasonal patterns with prolonged summer stratification and mixed conditions during other periods, providing a context for evaluating the forecasting models' performance.

FCR is primarily fed by a tri butary that receives water from upgradient Beaverdam Reservoir (BVR; Fig. 1) Both reservoirs develop hypolimnetic anoxia in response to thermal stratification between April and October and have similar catchment land use history and water chemistry (Gerling et al. 2016). During the summer stratified period, phytoplankton blooms and elevated concentrations of Fe, Mn, and P associated with hypolimnetic anoxia have been documented in FCR (Gerling et al. 2014, 2016). Hypolimnetic concentrations of nitrate þ nitrite and sulfate in FCR are less than 100 l g/L and 200 l g/L, respectively (Gerling et al., 2016; Munger, 2016).

2.4. Calibration and Analysis Approach

2.4.1. State Variable Observations

Temperature and dissolved oxygen depth profiles were recorded in FCR from 2013 to 2021 at the reservoir's deepest site and were retrieved from the Environmental Data Initiative Repository (Carey, Lewis, et al., 2022). In short, temperature and dissolved oxygen depth profiles were collected with a CTD (Conductivity, Temperature, and Depth) profiler fitted with a SBE 43 Dissolved Oxygen sensor. In addition, discrete depth profiles of temperature and dissolved oxygen were also collected with YSI water quality probes at approximately 1-m intervals (Carey, Wander, et al., 2022). Samples were collected at the deepest site of FCR (near the dam), and other inreservoir transects approximately monthly from October to February, fortnightly from March to May, and weekly from June to September. The YSI temperature profiles complement and fill in for missing CTD data. The observed temperature and dissolved oxygen profile data were spatially interpolated among depths on the data collection days to fill in for missing data and to achieve higher spatial resolution for the calculation of system metrics. Data manipulation, analysis, visualization and computations were undertaken in R (version: 4.1.2).

Dissolved oxygen conditions

The water column in FCR began to stratify in April of 2014 and 2015 and remained stratified until October in both years (Fig. S 2). Prior to April in each year, DO concentrations and temperature were relatively uniform with depth through the water column in FCR. By mid-April in each year, a thermocline developed between the warmer, top  4 m in the water column and deeper, cooler water. The temperature gradient persisted between April and October in both years, during which time we observed greater DO consumption in the hypolimnion in the absence of oxygenation.

By manipulating the HOx system, we substantially altered DO concentrations in the hypolimnion of FCR during the summer stratified periods in 2014 and 2015 (Fig. 3). When the HOx system was deactivated in 2014 and 2015, the volume-weighted mean hypolimnion (VWH) DO concentration rapidly decreased at a mean rate of 0.16 ± 0.04 mg/L/d in both years (1 SD; Fig. 3). When the HOx system was activated, the VWH DO concentration increased at a mean rate of 0.04 ± 0.03 mg/L/d in both years. DO concentrations rapidly homogenized throughout the hypolimnion due to mixing induced by the HOx system.

Operation of the HOx system prevented the development of anoxic conditions above the sediment -water interface (Fig. 3). DO rapidly depleted above the sediments when the HOx system was deactivated, which resulted in anoxic conditions at the bottom waters during 2 periods in the summer of 2014 and one period in the summer of 2015. During the 2 deactivation periods in summer 2014, anoxic conditions developed above the sediments within a week after deactivation. We continuously operated the HOx system for most of the summer stratified period in 2015 and anoxic conditions above the sediments were only observed (Fig. 3) during a 1-week period of deactivation in early June 2015. Oxic conditions persisted above the sediments whenever the HOx system was activated.

RESULTS

The reservoirs exhibited typical seasonality in their ecological dynamics over the >4-year time series (Figure 3). Every year, thermal stratification set-up in mid-March to early April, with fall mixing starting in late October to early November, and intermittent ice in December to March in both reservoirs. Although Tw in both the surface and bottom waters was similar in the two reservoirs, bottom-water DO in FCR exhibited fewer days of summer anoxia than in BVR due to oxygenation, especially during the summers of 2023 and 2024. Median Sp Cond was 10 μ S/cm higher in FCR than BVR, and both reservoirs displayed seasonal patterns of higher Sp Cond values in autumn and winter and lower values in spring and summer. On average, f DOM and Chl a concentrations were 1.5 and 2.2 times higher in FCR than BVR, respectively, with a higher frequency of intermittent phytoplankton blooms (>20 μ g/L) in FCR over the time series, especially in 2023 and 2024 (Figure 3).

Although intrinsic predictability was generally low for all variables, it was still significantly higher than white noise ( p ≤ 0.042, Appendix S 1: Table S 3, Figure S 2), indicating complex yet predictable dynamics. Aggregated across the entire time series, whole-period 1-PE ranged between 0.004 and 0.36 among variables (Appendix S 1: Table S 3).

Seasonally, Secchi disk depths were slightly deeper in CCR (4.0  0.8 m, 1 SD) compared to GWR (3.3  0.4 m) and BVR (2.8  0.7 m; Table 1). Additionally, TN, TP, and chlorophyll a concentrations were slightly lower in CCR compared to GWR and BVR seasonally (Table 1).

Further, the SHAP analyses provided valuable information on the directionality and importance of predictors. In BVR (Figure 4 b), higher DOM concentrations (dark purple) and low to moderate Schmidt stability (yellowgreen) were associated with higher chlorophyll-a. Moreover, low DOY harmonic values corresponding to late summer to early fall (see Figure S 2 in Supporting Information S 1) were also associated with higher chlorophyll-a. In FCR (Figure 4 d), higher Deep DO and higher DOM were associated with higher chlorophyll-a. Low to moderate DOY harmonic values indicating an earlier summer onset (Figure S 2 in Supporting Information S 1) extending into autumn were also associated with higher chlorophyll-a. Notably, low to moderate Schmidt stability in BVR and higher Schmidt stability in FCR were linked to higher SHAP values, highlighting the varying roles of stratification in phytoplankton promotion. Across both reservoirs, DOM showed a consistent positive association with model predictions, underscoring its key role in regulating phytoplankton dynamics. The wide dispersion of SHAP values for DOM indicates strong context dependence, with effects modulated by the growth environment, including thermal stratification, mixing regimes, light availability, and seasonal and thermal conditions.

3.3.2. SHAP Dependency Analyses

Site-specific SHAP main effect patterns revealed distinct predictor-response relationships for phytoplankton dynamics in FCR and BVR (Figure 5). At BVR, Schmidt Stability exhibited a clear non-linear influence on phytoplankton (Figure 5 a). The strongest positive effect (SHAP values up to 3.0) occurred under well-mixed conditions at very low stability ( < 20 J/m 2 ). As stratification streng thened (10-80 J/m 2 ), the contri bution of Schmidt stability became consistently negative or neutral, thereby limiting phytoplankton growth.

2.2. Study Sites and Monitoring Data

Our three study reservoirs near Roanoke, Virginia, USA, are owned and operated by the Western Virginia Water Authority as primary or secondary drinking water sources. Beaverdam Reservoir (BVR) is a small (0.39 km 2 ), shallow ( Z max at full pond = 13.0 m) eutrophic reservoir located in Vinton, Virginia (37.31°N, 79.82°W; Lofton et al., 2019). BVR drains into Falling Creek Reservoir (FCR), a second small (0.12 km 2 ), shallow ( Z max = 9.3 m at full pond) eutrophic reservoir located in Vinton, Virginia (37.30°N, 79.84°W; Lofton et al., 2019). Both BVR and FCR are dimictic reservoirs that thermally stratify from March through October and experience intermittent ice between December and February (Carey & Breef-Pilz, 2025 a, 2025 b). Carvins Cove Reservoir (CCR) is a warm monomictic, mesotrophic reservoir that is slightly larger (2.5 km 2 ) and deeper ( Z max at full pond = 23 m) than the other two reservoirs. CCR is thermally stratified between March and November each year (Carey, Breef-Pilz, & Howard, 2025). All three reservoirs are located within 15 km of each other, have primarily forested deciduous watersheds (Figure 1), and were constructed in 1872 (BVR), 1898 (FCR), and 1946 (CCR). Each reservoir experiences variable hydrology and water residence time, with residence times of ∼ 215 days in FCR, ∼ 330 days in BVR, and up to 642 days in CCR (Doubek et al., 2018; Howard et al., 2021). BVR and CCR receive the majority of their flow from forested headwater streams, while FCR receives the majority of its flow from a stream that drains from BVR (Figure 1 b). FCR and BVR are both eutrophic reservoirs with a trophic state index (TSI) of 55 and 50, respectively, while CCR is mesotrophic with a TSI of 39 (Carey, Breef-Pilz, Wander, et al., 2025; Carey et al., 2024; Carlson & Simpson, 1996).

items.answer:
The lowest observed Secchi value at BVR is 0.40 meters, based on the all-time historical sensor record across all available years and depths [5].

3.2. ML Models Performance and Configuration

Taylor diagrams indicate that all ML models per formed comparably at BVR and FCR, with slightly more variability in model per formance at FCR. Overall, the models were effective in capturing phytoplankton dynamics across both reservoirs. In BVR, Pearson's r had values between 0.84 and 0.86, and the RMSE values ranged from 2.4 to 2.5 μg/L (Figure S 3 in Supporting Information S 1). In FCR, the model per formance exhibited r values ranging from 0.81 to 0.83 and RMSE values between 6.6 and 6.9 μg/L (Figure S 3 in Supporting Information S 1). XGBoost achieved the lowest RMSE at both sites (FCR = 6.6 μg/L; BVR = 2.4 μg/L), demonstrating a robust and consistent per formance across sites, and was therefore selected as the reference model for this study. The hyperparameters used for the XGBoost model at each site are provided in Table S 1 in Supporting Information S 1.

Activation of the HOx system in FCR generated well-oxygenated conditions in the hypolimnion and anoxic conditions in the metalimnion, all while maintaining thermal stratification (Figure 3 A, C). In contrast, BVR's hypolimnion became anoxic soon after the onset of thermal stratification in May and remained anoxic through the sampling period; the metalimnion became anoxic from 11 August to 27 September (Figure 3 B, D). BVR's seasonal mean thermocline depth was similar to FCR's thermocline throughout the monitoring period (5.3 ± 1.0 m (1 S.D.) vs. 5.8 ± 1.0 m, respectively). Both reservoirs' epilimnia remained oxic during the sampling period (DO ‡ 6.3 mg l -1 ). Fall turnover in FCR occurred on 9 October, while turnover had not occurred yet in BVR by the end of the monitoring period on 21 October (Figure 3 A, B).

The well-oxygenated conditions in FCR's hypolimnion resulted in higher mean ORP values (210 ± 38 m V) in comparison with BVR's anoxic hypolimnion ( -90 ± 63 m V; Figure 4). BVR's hypolimnion reached its lowest ORP value of -155 m V on 23 August. We observed the lowest ORP in FCR's metalimnion on 2 September (0 m V), the same date as the lowest DO concentration (5 m, Figures 3 C and 4 A). This was the lowest ORP value observed among all of FCR's layers throughout the monitoring period. Conversely, BVR's metalimnion remained ‡ 20 m V during the monitoring period, despite becoming anoxic for 1 month (Figures 3 D and 4 B). FCR and BVR's seasonal mean epilimnetic ORP was similar during the sampling period (170 ± 75 m V and 190 ± 83 m V, respectively).

items.answer:
Dissolved oxygen at Falling Creek's 9 m hypolimnion is currently 7.07 mg/L, which is above the seasonal mean and well within the historical range for this time of year [5][7]. Reservoir literature confirms that if the hypolimnion becomes anoxic, internal release of phosphorus and iron/manganese from sediments can increase. Specifically, studies at Falling Creek and similar systems show that anoxia in bottom waters promotes the release of these nutrients and metals, while hypolimnetic oxygenation can suppress their mobilization [3][4][6][10]. This process is well-documented and is a key reason for operating hypolimnetic oxygenation systems [2][3].

High-frequency data were collected during two key periods: the natural reservoir turnover in fall 2020 and the initiation of HOx operation. These deployments captured variations in DO concentrations, water temperature, and stratification, providing insights into the reservoir's oxygenation dynamics under both natural and managed conditions.

3.1 | Observational data from whole- ecosystem manipulations

Injection of oxygen into the bottom waters of Falling Creek Reservoir (FCR) over 7 years increased the reservoir's observed hypolimnetic oxygen, resulting in substantial changes in total and dissolved C, N, and P concentrations (Figure 3 , Figure S 2). Due to the nature of our oxygenation manipulation, some years experienced low levels of oxygenation (i.e., the HOx was off for prolonged periods throughout the summer), while others experienced high levels of oxygenation during the stratified period (Figure 3 b ). Oxygenation resulted in substantially higher hypolimnetic oxygen concentrations without altering water temperature and thermal stratification in the reservoir (Figure 3 a,b). In 2019, oxygenation did not increase hypolimnetic oxygen concentrations to the same extent as preceding summers, likely because the HOx was only operated for intermittent 2- week periods (vs. 4- week or longer periods in all other years).

ABSTRACT

Climate change is predicted to have widespread impacts on freshwater lake and reservoir nutrient budgets by altering both hypolimnetic hypoxia and runoff, which will in turn alter the magnitude of internal and external nutrient loads. To examine the effects of these potential climate scenarios on nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P) budgets, we conducted a whole-catchment manipulation of hypolimnetic oxygen conditions and external loads to Falling Creek Reservoir (FCR), an old, eutrophic reservoir in a reforested catchment with a history of agricultural land use. Throughout 2 years of monitoring, internal N and P loading during hypoxic conditions dominated the hypolimnetic mass of nutrients in FCR, regardless of changes in external loading. FCR commonly functioned as a net sink of N and P, except during hypoxic conditions, when the reservoir was a net source of ammonium (NH þ 4 ) to downstream. We observed extremely high nitrate-nitrite (NO � 3 � NO � 2 ), soluble reactive P (SRP), total nitrogen (TN), and total phosphorus (TP) retention rates, indicating that the reservoir served as a sink for greater than 70% of NO � 3 � NO � 2 inputs and greater than 30% of SRP, TN, and TP inputs, on average. Our study is notable in the length of time since reforestation ( > 80 years) that a reservoir is still exhibiting high N and P internal loading during hypoxia, potentially as a result of the considerable store of accumulated nutrients in its sediment from historical agricultural runoff. Our whole-catchment manipulations highlight the importance of underst anding how multiple aspects of global change, waterbody and catchment characteristics, and land use history will interact to alter nutrient budgets in the future.

items.answer:
Surface chlorophyll-a at Falling Creek Reservoir is currently well below the 20 µg/L bloom threshold, and the 7-day forecast indicates a low but gradually increasing risk of exceeding this threshold. Studies identify dissolved organic matter, day of year, and water temperature as the dominant drivers of phytoplankton blooms.

**Supporting evidence:**
- The most recent available data (2026-06-28) show surface chlorophyll-a at 1.6 m is 4.57 µg/L, which is below both the 20 µg/L bloom threshold and the seasonal mean (10.08 µg/L), and falls well within the historical seasonal range (1.52–70.18 µg/L) [3][4].
- Over the past four days, chlorophyll-a values have ranged from 4.57 to 11.77 µg/L, always below the bloom threshold and within the historical window [3][5][6][8].
- The 7-day forecast projects a gradual rise in mean chlorophyll-a from 11.46 µg/L (day 1) to 14.57 µg/L (day 7). The probability of exceeding 20 µg/L is 0% on day 1, 4% on day 3, 10% on day 5, and 17% on day 7, indicating a low but increasing risk of bloom conditions by the end of the forecast period [1].
- Literature on Falling Creek Reservoir identifies dissolved organic matter, day of year harmonic, and water temperature as the dominant drivers of phytoplankton blooms [2]. Additional studies note that temporal variability in chlorophyll-a often exceeds spatial variability, and that cyanobacteria can dominate the phytoplankton community by biomass [11][12].

**Literature on anoxia and carbon cycling:**  
- Literature confirms that maintaining hypolimnetic oxygen above 8 mg/L prevents anoxia and reduces methane accumulation, while anoxic conditions increase methane and alter carbon dioxide cycling [4][3].  
- Oxygenation experiments in Falling Creek Reservoir increased aerobic respiration and CO₂ accumulation, while anoxia led to higher methane production [3][4][7].

contexts: Falling Creek Reservoir (FCR) is equipped with a hypolimnetic oxygenation system (HOx) that was operated during summer stratification from 2016 to mid-2018 to prevent hypolimnetic anoxia without affecting thermal stratification. In contrast, Beaverdam Reservoir (BVR) lacks a HOx system and consistently experiences hypolimnetic anoxia during summer. The HOx maintained dissolved oxygen levels above 8 mg/L in FCR's hypolimnion, whereas BVR's hypolimnion remained anoxic (<1 mg/L). After HOx deactivation in FCR in late July 2018, hypolimnetic anoxia and increased methane concentrations were observed, with BVR showing much higher greenhouse gas levels overall.

The study compared the effects of hypolimnetic oxygenation in Falling Creek Reservoir (FCR) with the naturally anoxic Beaverdam Reservoir (BVR). Oxygenation in FCR maintained oxic conditions, promoting aerobic respiration and higher CO2 accumulation, while BVR experienced sequential depletion of electron acceptors and increased methane production under anoxia. Alternate terminal electron acceptor pathways, including manganese and iron reduction, also contributed to organic carbon mineralization in FCR, influencing greenhouse gas dynamics until lake turnover.

The study investigated the effects of hypolimnetic oxygenation (HOx) and epilimnetic mixing (EM) on greenhouse gas dynamics in Falling Creek Reservoir, finding that HOx increased aerobic respiration and CO2 accumulation in the hypolimnion due to sediment organic carbon decomposition. Despite influencing seasonal methane and CO2 levels, these engineered systems did not conclusively increase overall reservoir greenhouse gas emissions. Field data from 2015 and 2016 showed variations in oxygen minimum zones and greenhouse gas concentrations linked to system operation and environmental factors like precipitation and inflow rates.

Studies show that hypolimnetic methane concentrations in lakes and reservoirs increase significantly during periods of anoxia, driven by low dissolved oxygen levels. Whole-ecosystem oxygenation experiments, such as those conducted in Falling Creek Reservoir with a hypolimnetic oxygenation system, demonstrate that maintaining oxygen levels above 8 mg/L prevents anoxia and reduces methane accumulation, whereas reservoirs without such systems experience persistent anoxia and elevated methane. These findings highlight the role of oxygenation in controlling greenhouse gas emissions from aquatic ecosystems amid environmental changes.

The study focuses on Falling Creek Reservoir (FCR) in Vinton, Virginia, a small eutrophic reservoir experiencing persistent hypolimnetic anoxia during summer stratification, leading to water quality issues. To address this, a side-stream hypolimnetic oxygenation system (HOx) was installed in 2012 to increase dissolved oxygen in the hypolimnion without disrupting thermal stratification. items.question: How strongly is Falling Creek currently thermally stratified (surface vs 9 m temperature), what does the forecast indicate for surface temperature this week, and what does the literature say about how stratification strength governs hypolimnetic oxygen depletion?
items.answer:
Falling Creek Reservoir is currently strongly thermally stratified, with a surface (0.1 m) temperature of 26.11 °C and a 9 m temperature of 9.97 °C on 2026-06-28—a difference of over 16 °C, indicating robust stratification typical for summer conditions at this site [3][4]. This stratification is consistent with historical patterns of summer stratification observed in the reservoir [1].

The 7-day forecast indicates that surface temperatures will remain high, with the most recent observation at 26.11 °C (0.1 m, 2026-06-28) and no forecasted probability of 9 m temperatures exceeding 25 °C; the 9 m forecast mean remains near 10 °C (range 8.09–13.05 °C) through the week [3][5][11]. This suggests continued strong stratification is expected.

Literature confirms that stratification strength governs hypolimnetic oxygen depletion: strong thermal stratification limits mixing between surface and bottom waters, restricting oxygen replenishment to the hypolimnion and promoting oxygen depletion and anoxia in deep layers [12][13]. Manipulation studies at Falling Creek Reservoir have shown that altering hypolimnetic oxygen conditions (e.g., via oxygenation) can substantially affect nutrient cycling and water quality, further underscoring the link between stratification, oxygen depletion, and ecosystem impacts [13][15].

Confidence: High. Sensor data are from 2026-06-28 (current), and forecast ensemble spread is moderate but does not affect the conclusion of persistent strong stratification. Literature consensus supports the mechanistic link between stratification and hypolimnetic oxygen depletion.

The study focuses on Falling Creek Reservoir (FCR) in Vinton, Virginia, a small eutrophic reservoir experiencing persistent hypolimnetic anoxia during summer stratification, leading to water quality issues. To address this, a side-stream hypolimnetic oxygenation system (HOx) was installed in 2012 to increase dissolved oxygen in the hypolimnion without disrupting thermal stratification. The research utilizes the open-source AED modeling library to simulate dissolved oxygen dynamics, supported by temperature and oxygen depth profile data collected from 2013 to 2021 for model calibration and analysis.

ABSTRACT

Climate change is predicted to have widespread impacts on freshwater lake and reservoir nutrient budgets by altering both hypolimnetic hypoxia and runoff, which will in turn alter the magnitude of internal and external nutrient loads. To examine the effects of these potential climate scenarios on nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P) budgets, we conducted a whole-catchment manipulation of hypolimnetic oxygen conditions and external loads to Falling Creek Reservoir (FCR), an old, eutrophic reservoir in a reforested catchment with a history of agricultural land use. Throughout 2 years of monitoring, internal N and P loading during hypoxic conditions dominated the hypolimnetic mass of nutrients in FCR, regardless of changes in external loading. FCR commonly functioned as a net sink of N and P, except during hypoxic conditions, when the reservoir was a net source of ammonium (NH þ 4 ) to downstream. We observed extremely high nitrate-nitrite (NO � 3 � NO � 2 ), soluble reactive P (SRP), total nitrogen (TN), and total phosphorus (TP) retention rates, indicating that the reservoir served as a sink for greater than 70% of NO � 3 � NO � 2 inputs and greater than 30% of SRP, TN, and TP inputs, on average. Our study is notable in the length of time since reforestation ( > 80 years) that a reservoir is still exhibiting high N and P internal loading during hypoxia, potentially as a result of the considerable store of accumulated nutrients in its sediment from historical agricultural runoff. Our whole-catchment manipulations highlight the importance of underst anding how multiple aspects of global change, waterbody and catchment characteristics, and land use history will interact to alter nutrient budgets in the future.

The study compared the effects of hypolimnetic oxygenation in Falling Creek Reservoir (FCR) with the naturally anoxic Beaverdam Reservoir (BVR). Oxygenation in FCR maintained oxic conditions, promoting aerobic respiration and higher CO2 accumulation, while BVR experienced sequential depletion of electron acceptors and increased methane production under anoxia. Alternate terminal electron acceptor pathways, including manganese and iron reduction, also contributed to organic carbon mineralization in FCR, influencing greenhouse gas dynamics until lake turnover.

Instead of using a single PM, as has been done in previous implementations of FLARE (Carey et al., 2022 b; Thomas et al., 2020, 2023), we used three different PMs, implemented via integration with Lake Ensembl R R software (LER; Moore et al., 2021), to answer question 1. These PMs were run inside the FLARE framework to generate a multi-model ensemble (MME) from the output (Figure 1), hereafter referred to as the PM MME forecast. To answer questions 2 and 3, two baseline models were also included to produce the full MME forecast (full MME, hereafter), which consisted of five individual models ( n = 3 PMs and n = 2 baseline models). Finally, these forecasts are evaluated using the in-situ water temperature observations (Figure 1) via a suite of metrics, described below.

2.2. Site Description and Data Collection

We generated water temperature forecasts for Falling Creek Reservoir (FCR), a eutrophic reservoir located in Vinton, Virginia, USA (37.30°N, 79.84°W). FCR is managed by the Western Virginia Water Authority as a drinking water source. The reservoir has a mean depth of 4 m and a maximum depth of 9.3 m, with a surface area of 0.12 km 2 (Carey et al., 2022 a). A dimictic system, FCR generally stratifies from May to October and has intermittent ice-cover from December to March (Carey & Breef-Pilz, 2023). The reservoir has one primary inflow and water level is maintained to be generally constant over time.

Between 2014 and 2016, Beaverdam Reservoir (BVR) experienced increasing hypolimnetic cyanobacterial blooms, with peak biomass rising each year and blooms occurring deeper below the thermocline during strong thermal stratification and hypolimnetic anoxia. Nutrient release from sediments, particularly total phosphorus (TP), total nitrogen (TN), soluble reactive phosphorus (SRP), and ammonium (NH4+), followed anoxia development and contributed to bloom formation. Cyanobacterial biomass was influenced by multiple factors including TP, TN, temperature, and light, with models incorporating these variables effectively predicting bloom dynamics at different depths. The warming of the hypolimnion over the years likely contributed to the increasing magnitude of cyanobacterial blooms.

Researchers developed and tested a forecasting framework for near-surface chlorophyll a concentrations in two Virginia reservoirs: Falling Creek Reservoir (FCR) and Beaverdam Reservoir (BVR). The model, initially trained on FCR data, was successfully scaled to BVR, producing accurate weekly forecasts with low root mean square errors, though with higher uncertainty at BVR. The study highlights the framework's transferability to new waterbodies, recommending site-specific model tuning and use of available data sources to improve predictions in ecosystems lacking extensive monitoring.

The studies on Beaverdam Reservoir (BVR) and Falling Creek Reservoir (FCR) reveal that temporal variability in biogeochemical variables such as nutrients and chlorophyll-a often exceeds spatial variability, challenging traditional reservoir continuum models. Both reservoirs generally act as sinks for nitrate and total phosphorus but sources for total nitrogen, dissolved organic carbon, and chlorophyll-a, with biogeochemical hotspots most consistently found at the stream-reservoir interface. Hydrological changes and reservoir management significantly influence nutrient dynamics and the spatial distribution of processing hotspots.

3.3. Model Interpretation With SHAP Analysis

3.3.1. Potential Drivers of Phytoplankton Dynamics in the Reservoirs

SHAPanalysis of the XGBoost models revealed varying drivers of phytoplankton in the two reservoirs (Figure 4). For example, in BVR, the most important predictors of phytoplankton dynamics, listed in descending order, were DOM, DOY Harmonic, Schmidt stability, and water temperature (Figure 4 a). In comparison, Deep DO, DOM, DOY Harmonic, and water temperature were the primary predictors of phytoplankton in FCR (Figure 4 c).

Seasonal and physicochemical drivers of chlorophyll-a variability were analyzed in Beaverdam (BVR) and Falling Creek (FCR) Reservoirs, revealing that dissolved organic matter (DOM), day of year (DOY) harmonic, and water temperature are key predictors. SHAP and partial dependence analyses showed that while both reservoirs share dominant drivers, site-specific factors like deep dissolved oxygen (DO) in FCR and Schmidt stability in BVR influence phytoplankton dynamics differently. Temperature and stratification interact to govern nutrient distribution and phytoplankton responses, with FCR exhibiting threshold-like summer blooms linked to warm, stratified conditions, highlighting complex nonlinear ecological responses.

Forecasts of near-surface chlorophyll a (chl a) at FCR were generated over approximately 600 days using daily, weekly, and fortnightly autoregressive models based on sensor data. Forecast performance was evaluated across the full period, during bloom and non-bloom conditions, with weekly and fortnightly forecasts generally outperforming or matching null persistence models, while daily forecasts did not outperform null models. Observed chl a showed substantial variability, including two major blooms and rapid declines due to copper sulfate treatments. A similar forecasting framework was applied at BVR, incorporating meteorological forecasts to drive chl a predictions.

Importantly, our study also shows that prolonged hypolimnetic anoxia in the summer decreases the ability of a reservoir to retain C, N, and P, substantially increasing the downstream export of these elements.

3.1 | Observational data from whole- ecosystem manipulations

Injection of oxygen into the bottom waters of Falling Creek Reservoir (FCR) over 7 years increased the reservoir's observed hypolimnetic oxygen, resulting in substantial changes in total and dissolved C, N, and P concentrations (Figure 3 , Figure S 2). Due to the nature of our oxygenation manipulation, some years experienced low levels of oxygenation (i.e., the HOx was off for prolonged periods throughout the summer), while others experienced high levels of oxygenation during the stratified period (Figure 3 b ). Oxygenation resulted in substantially higher hypolimnetic oxygen concentrations without altering water temperature and thermal stratification in the reservoir (Figure 3 a,b). In 2019, oxygenation did not increase hypolimnetic oxygen concentrations to the same extent as preceding summers, likely because the HOx was only operated for intermittent 2- week periods (vs. 4- week or longer periods in all other years).

The water column in FCR began to stratify in April of 2014 and 2015 and remained stratified until October in both years (Fig. S 2). Prior to April in each year, DO concentrations and temperature were relatively uniform with depth through the water column in FCR. By mid-April in each year, a thermocline developed between the warmer, top  4 m in the water column and deeper, cooler water. The temperature gradient persisted between April and October in both years, during which time we observed greater DO consumption in the hypolimnion in the absence of oxygenation.

By manipulating the HOx system, we substantially altered DO concentrations in the hypolimnion of FCR during the summer stratified periods in 2014 and 2015 (Fig. 3). When the HOx system was deactivated in 2014 and 2015, the volume-weighted mean hypolimnion (VWH) DO concentration rapidly decreased at a mean rate of 0.16 ± 0.04 mg/L/d in both years (1 SD; Fig. 3). When the HOx system was activated, the VWH DO concentration increased at a mean rate of 0.04 ± 0.03 mg/L/d in both years. DO concentrations rapidly homogenized throughout the hypolimnion due to mixing induced by the HOx system.

Operation of the HOx system prevented the development of anoxic conditions above the sediment -water interface (Fig. 3). DO rapidly depleted above the sediments when the HOx system was deactivated, which resulted in anoxic conditions at the bottom waters during 2 periods in the summer of 2014 and one period in the summer of 2015. During the 2 deactivation periods in summer 2014, anoxic conditions developed above the sediments within a week after deactivation. We continuously operated the HOx system for most of the summer stratified period in 2015 and anoxic conditions above the sediments were only observed (Fig. 3) during a 1-week period of deactivation in early June 2015. Oxic conditions persisted above the sediments whenever the HOx system was activated.

items.answer:

**Supporting evidence:**

**Confidence:**  
High. The forecast ensemble is consistent, the most recent sensor data is current (0 days old), and literature supports forecast reliability for this horizon. There is no signal of an impending bloom or threshold exceedance, but as always, continued monitoring is warranted to detect rapid changes.

Q 4: Forecast scalability to new locations

Our forecast model framework was successfully scaled from FCR to BVR, producing weekly forecasts of surface chl a at both sites from August 2020 -August 2021. Forecasts at BVR matched well with observed chl a at both the 1-week and 2-week horizon (RMSE = 2.44 μ g/L; 3.07 μ g/L, respectively), with a small decline in per formance up to the 2-week forecast horizon (Figure 6 a,b). All forecasts at BVR showed very high uncertainty around the forecast mean throughout the forecast time period. Forecasts of chl a at FCR over the same time period (RMSE = 5.36 μ g/ L; 5.16 μ g/L) were less accurate but had lower overall uncertainty (Figure 6 c,d).

While process uncertainty is still by far the largest contri butor of overall uncertainty (Figure 7) in forecasts for FCR and BVR, parameter uncertainty had a higher contri bution in BVR than in FCR. Additionally, while the overall contri bution is much lower, both BVR and FCR show a slight increase in weather driver uncertainty over the late spring to mid-summer time period (  February to August). Discharge driver uncertainty remained a very small contri bution to overall uncertainty in FCR but was negligible in BVR. Total variance between the two sites was similar at both 1-week and 2-week forecast horizons.

ECOLOGICAL APPLICATIONS

In summary, to produce weekly forecasts of chl a at BVR, we followed the same framework as at FCR (see Methods: Forecasting Framework ), resulting in 1-week and 2-week forecasts every day from 1 August 2020 to 31 August 2021. On each day a forecast was made, all available observational data up to the day being forecasted were used to fit the model in a Bayesian framework. We then used forecasts of shortwave radiation from NOAA GEFS, as well as NOAA GEFS forecasts of precipitation to drive the TWMB inflow model, to drive our chl a forecasts. Additionally, we produced 1-week and 2-week forecasts at FCR over this same period and conducted a full uncertainty analysis for both FCR and BVR to compare the relative per formance of the forecast model at both sites.

Researchers developed and tested a forecasting framework for near-surface chlorophyll a concentrations in two Virginia reservoirs: Falling Creek Reservoir (FCR) and Beaverdam Reservoir (BVR). The model, initially trained on FCR data, was successfully scaled to BVR, producing accurate weekly forecasts with low root mean square errors, though with higher uncertainty at BVR. The study highlights the framework's transferability to new waterbodies, recommending site-specific model tuning and use of available data sources to improve predictions in ecosystems lacking extensive monitoring.

Seasonal and physicochemical drivers of chlorophyll-a variability were analyzed in Beaverdam (BVR) and Falling Creek (FCR) Reservoirs, revealing that dissolved organic matter (DOM), day of year (DOY) harmonic, and water temperature are key predictors. SHAP and partial dependence analyses showed that while both reservoirs share dominant drivers, site-specific factors like deep dissolved oxygen (DO) in FCR and Schmidt stability in BVR influence phytoplankton dynamics differently. Temperature and stratification interact to govern nutrient distribution and phytoplankton responses, with FCR exhibiting threshold-like summer blooms linked to warm, stratified conditions, highlighting complex nonlinear ecological responses.

The studies on Beaverdam Reservoir (BVR) and Falling Creek Reservoir (FCR) reveal that temporal variability in biogeochemical variables such as nutrients and chlorophyll-a often exceeds spatial variability, challenging traditional reservoir continuum models. Both reservoirs generally act as sinks for nitrate and total phosphorus but sources for total nitrogen, dissolved organic carbon, and chlorophyll-a, with biogeochemical hotspots most consistently found at the stream-reservoir interface. Hydrological changes and reservoir management significantly influence nutrient dynamics and the spatial distribution of processing hotspots.

Challenges in forecasting phytoplankton blooms

Forecast accuracy differed between the July 2019 and March/April 2020 bloom events, indicating that phytoplankton dynamics during some blooms may be more predictable than others. It is possible that the differences in predictive ability between blooms may be because of different phytoplankton taxa underlying the two blooms, but unfortunately we do not have the data to test this hypo thesis (Appendix S 1: Section S 5). However, all forecast models better predicted the March/April 2020 bloom than the July 2019 bloom (maximum concentration = 55.7 μ g/L), likely because the March/April 2020 bloom was much lower in peak concentrations (maximum concentration = 24.2 μ g/ L), and lasted a longer period of time, allowing the forecasts to adjust to elevated chl a concentrations (see Appendix S 1: Figures S 6 -S 8 show dramatic changes in parameter values in response to bloom events).

items.question: Taking the upper end of the 95% ensemble range, how warm could the 9 m water temperature in FCR get over the 7-day FLARE forecast?
items.answer:

The most recent observation is current as of 2026-06-28, and the forecast ensemble spread is moderate, supporting a robust upper-limit estimate.

In addition to meteorology forecasts, one model (TS AR) required forecasts of water temperature. We used water temperature forecasts generated from the Forecasting Lake And Reservoir Ecosystems (FLARE) forecasting system, which has generated 1 to 34 days-ahead water temperature forecasts for FCR from 2018-present, BVR from 2020-present, and CCR from 2022 to present (Thomas et al., 2020; Wander et al., 2024). FLARE has high accuracy across waterbodies with RMSE (root mean square error) and CRPS (continuous rank probability score) values less than 2°C up to a 35-day horizon in our study reservoirs (Thomas et al., 2020; Wander et al., 2024), as well as high accuracy in lakes across the United States (Thomas et al., 2023). FLARE uses a one-dimensional process-based hydrodynamic model (the General Lake Model; Hipsey et al., 2019), to forecast the water temperature of different water layers using forecasted meteorology (NOAA GEFS) and hydrology driver data. FLARE provides water temperature forecasts at a 0.5-m resolution throughout the water column, from which we used the forecasts for the 1.5 m depth in each reservoir to correspond with the depth of the deployed f DOM sensors (Howard et al., 2025 b).

2.2. Site Description and Data Collection

We generated water temperature forecasts for Falling Creek Reservoir (FCR), a eutrophic reservoir located in Vinton, Virginia, USA (37.30°N, 79.84°W). FCR is managed by the Western Virginia Water Authority as a drinking water source. The reservoir has a mean depth of 4 m and a maximum depth of 9.3 m, with a surface area of 0.12 km 2 (Carey et al., 2022 a). A dimictic system, FCR generally stratifies from May to October and has intermittent ice-cover from December to March (Carey & Breef-Pilz, 2023). The reservoir has one primary inflow and water level is maintained to be generally constant over time.

The FLARE forecasting system is an automated, open-source tool designed to predict water temperature in lakes and reservoirs with high accuracy, achieving an average RMSE of 1.4°C over a 16-day horizon across various thermal conditions. It uses data assimilation to update sensitive model parameters and is robust even when short-term data gaps occur. While currently limited by simplified inflow and outflow modeling and reliance on a 1-D hydrodynamic model, FLARE’s scalable framework supports future enhancements and integration with ecosystem models for broader water quality forecasting applications.

items.question: How will the probability that surface chlorophyll-a at FCR exceeds the 20 µg/L bloom threshold change over the 7-day FLARE forecast?
items.answer:
The probability that surface chlorophyll-a at FCR will exceed the 20 µg/L bloom threshold is forecast to increase gradually over the next 7 days, but remains below 20% throughout the period.

Supporting evidence:  
- The most recent available sensor data (2026-06-28) shows a Chla_ugL_mean of 4.57 µg/L at 1.6 m, well below the 20 µg/L threshold and also below the seasonal mean, though still within the historical range for this time of year [3][4].  
- The FLARE 7-day forecast projects the following daily probabilities for exceeding 20 µg/L at 1.6 m:  
  - Day 1: 0%  
  - Day 3: 4%  
  - Day 5: 10%  
  - Day 7: 17%  
  These probabilities are not cumulative; each is the chance on that specific day. The ensemble mean forecast for day 7 is 14.57 µg/L, with the upper range reaching 29.76 µg/L, indicating some risk but not a high likelihood of a bloom event [1].

Interpretation:  
The probability of exceeding the bloom threshold starts at zero and rises to 17% by day 7, reflecting a modest but increasing risk. Most forecast ensemble members remain below the threshold, but a minority reach or exceed it, driving the upward trend in probability.

Confidence:  
Confidence is moderate. The forecast is based on a large ensemble (221 members) and recent sensor data, but ensemble spread increases with lead time (from 4.77 to 13.37 µg/L), indicating growing uncertainty further out [1][3]. The current low chlorophyll-a levels support the low short-term risk, but the rising probability warrants continued monitoring.

The studies on Beaverdam Reservoir (BVR) and Falling Creek Reservoir (FCR) reveal that temporal variability in biogeochemical variables such as nutrients and chlorophyll-a often exceeds spatial variability, challenging traditional reservoir continuum models. Both reservoirs generally act as sinks for nitrate and total phosphorus but sources for total nitrogen, dissolved organic carbon, and chlorophyll-a, with biogeochemical hotspots most consistently found at the stream-reservoir interface. Hydrological changes and reservoir management significantly influence nutrient dynamics and the spatial distribution of processing hotspots.

Seasonal and physicochemical drivers of chlorophyll-a variability were analyzed in Beaverdam (BVR) and Falling Creek (FCR) Reservoirs, revealing that dissolved organic matter (DOM), day of year (DOY) harmonic, and water temperature are key predictors. SHAP and partial dependence analyses showed that while both reservoirs share dominant drivers, site-specific factors like deep dissolved oxygen (DO) in FCR and Schmidt stability in BVR influence phytoplankton dynamics differently. Temperature and stratification interact to govern nutrient distribution and phytoplankton responses, with FCR exhibiting threshold-like summer blooms linked to warm, stratified conditions, highlighting complex nonlinear ecological responses.

3. Results

3.1. Chlorophyll-a Variability at FCR and BVR

Seasonal and temporal analyses of Chl-a concentrations revealed greater variability and bloom intensity in FCR than in BVR (Figure 3). Monthly boxplots (Figure 3 a) show clear seasonal patterns at both sites, with elevated Chl-a levels during summer (June-September) and generally reduced levels in winter (December-February). Unlike BVR, FCR exhibited elevated Chl-a concentrations that persisted through late autumn and early winter (November-December). During this period, the median values ranged from 15 to 18 μg/L, with occasional peaks reaching up to 60 μg/L, indicating winter bloom events. In contrast, BVR maintained relatively low Chl-a levels in winter, typically ≤ 10 μg/L. During warmer periods (June-September), peak median values reached ∼ 18 μg/L at FCRand ∼ 15 μg/L at BVR. FCR exhibited greater variability and a higher frequency of bloom events, with values occasionally exceeding 100 μg/L (Figure 3 b). BVR displayed more consistent, moderate Chl-a variability, typically ranging between 5 and 30 μg/L, with the highest Chl-a values of ∼ 33 μg/L. These results highlight pronounced seasonal bloom dynamics and greater interannual bloom frequency and intensity in FCR relative to BVR, suggesting site-specific drivers.

Forecast evaluation

To address Q 1, we evaluated our forecasts ' per formance post-hoc for three time periods: (1) the entire  600-day period during which multiple forecasts were produced at FCR, (2) non-bloom conditions, and (3) bloom conditions. Bloom conditions were determined as any time when observed chl a concentrations were above a bloom threshold. The threshold for bloom conditions was determined as four times the SD of historical chl a at FCR from CTD chl a data set (17.1 μ g/L; Carey et al., 2019). We chose four SDs as our threshold, rather than three SDs (e.g., Healy, 1979), because of the high-frequency nature of our sensor data, which may increase the likelihood of outliers due to sensor fouling and phytoplankton quenching (Hamilton et al., 2010; Mc Bride & Rose, 2018; Rousso et al., 2021). Forecasts were evaluated as occurring under bloom conditions any time the observed chl a was above this threshold on the day the forecast was initiated or any days when chl a was above this threshold within the 14-day forecast horizon. Challenges in forecasting phytoplankton blooms

Forecast accuracy differed between the July 2019 and March/April 2020 bloom events, indicating that phytoplankton dynamics during some blooms may be more predictable than others. It is possible that the differences in predictive ability between blooms may be because of different phytoplankton taxa underlying the two blooms, but unfortunately we do not have the data to test this hypo thesis (Appendix S 1: Section S 5). However, all forecast models better predicted the March/April 2020 bloom than the July 2019 bloom (maximum concentration = 55.7 μ g/L), likely because the March/April 2020 bloom was much lower in peak concentrations (maximum concentration = 24.2 μ g/ L), and lasted a longer period of time, allowing the forecasts to adjust to elevated chl a concentrations (see Appendix S 1: Figures S 6 -S 8 show dramatic changes in parameter values in response to bloom events).

items.question: Over the 7-day FLARE forecast for FCR, how will surface water temperature at 1.6 m compare with 20 °C and 25 °C?
items.answer:
Over the 7-day FLARE forecast for FCR, surface water temperature at 1.6 m is expected to rise from below 25 °C to above 25 °C, with a high probability of exceeding 25 °C by the end of the forecast period.

Supporting evidence:
- The most recent available sensor data (2026-06-28) shows a temperature of 23.17 °C at 1.6 m, which is below both 20 °C and 25 °C and within the typical seasonal range (seasonal mean: 24.46 °C; range: 16.52–30.58 °C) [4].
- The FLARE 7-day forecast projects a steady increase:  
  - Day 1: mean 23.32 °C (2% chance >25 °C)  
  - Day 3: mean 24.53 °C (38% chance >25 °C)  
  - Day 5: mean 26.01 °C (71% chance >25 °C)  
  - Day 7: mean 26.98 °C (86% chance >25 °C)  
  This indicates a low probability of exceeding 25 °C in the next 1–3 days, but a high probability (71–86%) by days 5–7. The mean forecast does not drop below 20 °C at any point; all ensemble members remain above this threshold throughout the period [1].
- Literature confirms that FLARE forecasts are typically accurate within ~1.4 °C at this depth and horizon [7][10].

Confidence: High. The forecast is recent, ensemble spread is moderate, and the system’s historical accuracy supports the outlook. However, actual temperatures could vary by ±1–3 °C due to forecast uncertainty, especially at longer lead times.

FLARE has high accuracy across waterbodies with RMSE (root mean square error) and CRPS (continuous rank probability score) values less than 2°C up to a 35-day horizon in our study reservoirs (Thomas et al., 2020; Wander et al., 2024), as well as high accuracy in lakes across the United States (Thomas et al., 2023). FLARE uses a one-dimensional process-based hydrodynamic model (the General Lake Model; Hipsey et al., 2019), to forecast the water temperature of different water layers using forecasted meteorology (NOAA GEFS) and hydrology driver data. FLARE provides water temperature forecasts at a 0.5-m resolution throughout the water column, from which we used the forecasts for the 1.5 m depth in each reservoir to correspond with the depth of the deployed f DOM sensors (Howard et al., 2025 b).

Observations were binned into 0.25 m depth intervals to match the vertical resolution of the FLARE forecast output. Measurements within the same bin were averaged together. These data were used in FLARE data assimilation and PM parameter tuning, as well as inputs to the two baseline models (see Section 2.3), and in forecast evaluation (Figure 1, Section 2.4).

Dates of the mixed and stratified periods were calculated based on the density difference between 1 m from surface (1 m) and ∼ 1 m above the bottom (8 m) of the lake, with a minimum density difference of 0.1 kg m 2 indicating that the lake was stratified (Wilson et al., 2020). The stratified period was defined as the summer period when continuous stratified conditions occurred and the mixed period as any time outside of this. In addition, the observed thermocline depth was estimated using the Lake Analyzer R package (Read et al., 2011).

We applied an interpretable machine learning framework (SHAP-XGBoost) to predict, identify, and understand the primary drivers of phytoplankton dynamics in two adjacent reservoirs. SHAP analyses revealed reservoirspecific predictor responses, emp hasizing the need for site-specific modeling strategies. Interestingly, interaction analyses showed that high surface temperatures ( > 25°C) combined with strong stratification promoted phytoplankton growth in FCR but not in BVR, revealing differing ecological responses to thermal conditions in neighboring reservoirs. Moreover, our findings indicate that phytoplankton biomass in FCR can be high during both mixed and stratified conditions, whereas phytoplankton biomass in BVR is primarily associated with wellmixed conditions. These insights can inform process-based modeling efforts and support the development of targeted, site-specific water quality management strategies. Furthermore, integrating relative stability analyses into our XAI workflow added a critical layer of validation, allowing us to assess the robustness of the feature attri butions. This framework enhances both scientific interpretation and supports management-oriented decisionmaking in freshwater systems. items.answer:
> **Operational check (LEADS-computed):** latest 9 m DO 7.07 mg/L (2026-06-28) is above the 4 mg/L HOx trigger → HOx activation **not indicated** on this reading. Forecast: P(DO < 4 mg/L) peaks at 43% (day 7 of 7).

Activation of the hypolimnetic oxygenation (HOx) system at FCR is not indicated on the current reading, but forecasted hypoxia risk increases later this week.

**Supporting evidence:**
- The most recent available data (2026-06-28) show hypolimnetic DO at 9 m is 7.07 mg/L, well above the operational activation threshold of 4 mg/L and above the seasonal mean, though still within the historical range [10][3]. This does not indicate a need for immediate activation, but high DO could reflect ongoing HOx operation; the system's current state is unknown [1].
- Near-term forecasts show low immediate risk: the 1-day forecast gives only a 1% chance of DO dropping below 4 mg/L [13], and the 3-day forecast gives a 14% chance [14].
- By day 5, the risk rises: the 5-day forecast shows a 30% probability of DO < 4 mg/L [16]. The 7-day forecast mean is 4.35 mg/L (range 0.73–7.81), with high ensemble spread, indicating substantial uncertainty and a real possibility of hypoxia developing later in the week [17].
- Forecast skill is strong at 3 days, marginal at 7 days, and weak beyond that, so confidence in the 5–7 day risk is moderate but not high [2].

**Confidence:** The current DO is healthy, so activation is not indicated on today's reading. However, there is a rising risk of hypoxia by day 5–7, with substantial forecast uncertainty. Re-evaluation with updated sensor data and forecasts is warranted mid-week.

Hypolimnetic oxygenation system (HOx)

FCR has a side-stream hypolimnetic oxygenation system (HOx; Fig. 1 B) that was installed to prevent hypolimnetic anoxia without altering thermal strati fi cation or water temperature (Gerling et al. 2014). HOx systems are increasingly used to prevent water quality impairment associated with anoxia (Preece et al. 2019). The HOx was operated during the summer-strati fi ed periods of 2016, 2017, and until 30 July in 2018 to maintain a well-oxygenated hypolimnion in FCR (Table SI.1). BVR also exhibits hypolimnetic anoxia but does not have a HOx system.

The Falling Creek Reservoir (FCR) in Vinton, VA, is equipped with a hypolimnetic oxygenation (HOx) system that can be activated to control dissolved oxygen (DO) levels in the hypolimnion without affecting thermal stratification. High-frequency data were collected during two key periods: the natural reservoir turnover in fall 2020 and the initiation of HOx operation. These deployments captured variations in DO concentrations, water temperature, and stratification, providing insights into the reservoir's oxygenation dynamics under both natural and managed conditions.

2.1.2. Hypolimnetic oxygenation (HOx) and epilimnetic mixing (EM) systems

In 2012, the WVWA deployed a side stream supersaturation HOx system and a bubble plume EM system in FCR to improve the water quality (Gerling et al., 2016, 2014; Munger et al., 2016). The HOx increases DO concentrations just above the sediments in the hypolimnion bypumpinghypolimnetic wateronshoreto anoxygen saturation chamber, where 95% pure oxygen gas is dissolved into the water. The supersaturated water is pumped back into the hypolimnion at the same depth from where it was extracted and is mixed throughout the entire hypolimnion while not disrupting thermal stratification or water temperature (Gerling et al., 2014). The well-oxygenated hypolimnion due to HOx operation prevents the release of reduced metals and nutrients from the sediments (Gerling et al., 2014; Munger et al., 2016). The EM injects bubbled air into the epilimnion and upper metalimnion of FCR to mix the surface waters and decrease cyanobacterial blooms (Chen et al., 2017, 2018). When the EM is deactivated, operation of the HOx streng thens the thermocline and thermal stratification of the reservoir, generating suitable conditions for organic carbon decomposition and the entrainment of inflowing low DO water from the sediments to create MOMs at the thermocline. The HOx is generally activated through the entire summer stratified period in FCR, while the EM is only activated intermittently as needed.

In September 2012, a side-stream supersaturation hypolimnetic oxygenation system (HOx) was installed in FCR to increase DO concentrations in the hypolimnion of the reservoir while maintaining thermal strati fi cation (see Gerling et al., 2014 for details on the HOx system). The HOx system consists of a submersible pump (at 8.5 m depth), inlet piping, an oxygen source, an oxygen contact chamber, and distri bution headers (at 8.5 m depth). Water is withdrawn from the reservoir via the pump, transferred to the oxygen contact chamber and supersaturated with oxygen. The water is then transported to the distri bution headers via the outlet piping, where it is injected back into the hypolimnion. Previous work (Gerling et al., 2014) and continued oxygen monitoring (Carey et al., 2019) demonstrate that during operation, the HOx system introduces oxygen into the hypolimnion while maintaining thermal strati fi cation.

2. Methods

2.1. Study site

Falling Creek Reservoir (FCR) is a shallow (maximum depth ¼ 9.3 m, mean depth ¼ 4 m, surface area ¼ 0.119 km 2 , volume of 3.1 -10 5 m at full pond), eutrophic drinking water reservoir owned and managed by the Western Virginia Water Authority (WVWA) and located in a forested watershed in southwestern Virginia, USA, as shown in Fig. 2. The primary source of water to the reservoir is a surface water stream that enters along the nor theastern shoreline (Gerling et al., 2016). FCR is moderately eutrophic and typically experiences thermal strati fi cation between April and October, during which time the hypolimnion develops anoxic conditions (Gerling et al., 2016, 2014).

Fig. 2. Falling Creek Reservoir bathymetry, location of oxygenation system diffuser lines, and water sample collection sites.

2.2. Hypolimnetic oxygenation system description

In autumn 2012, a side-stream supersaturation hypolimnetic oxygenation system was deployed in FCR (see Gerling et al., 2014, for a full system description and analysis of reservoir oxygen demand). The HOx system at FCR consists of a submersible pump (positioned at 8.5 m depth), inlet piping, an oxygen source, an oxygen contact chamber, outlet piping, and distri bution headers (positioned at 8.5 m depth). Water is withdrawn from the reservoir via the submersible pump and transferred to the oxygen contact chamber, where it is supersaturated with oxygen supplied by the oxygen source. The water is then transported to the distri bution headers via the outlet piping, where it is injected back into the hypolimnion. A schematic showing the side-stream supersaturation HOx system in FCR is depicted in Fig. 1.

items.question: Should we dose algaecide at FCR given current and forecast chlorophyll-a conditions?
items.answer:
> **Operational check (LEADS-computed):** latest 1.6 m chl-a 4.57 µg/L (2026-06-28) is below the 20 µg/L bloom threshold → bloom control **not indicated** on this reading. Forecast: P(chl-a > 20 µg/L) peaks at 17% (day 7 of 7).

Algaecide dosing at FCR is not indicated based on current and forecast chlorophyll-a conditions.

**Supporting sensor and forecast evidence:**  
- The most recent available data (2026-06-28) shows chlorophyll-a at 1.6 m is 4.57 µg/L, well below the operational threshold of 20 µg/L for algaecide consideration. This value is also below the seasonal mean and within the historical range for this time of year [3][6][7].
- The FLARE 1-day forecast projects a mean chlorophyll-a of 11.46 µg/L (range 7.04–16.58), with a 0% probability of exceeding the 20 µg/L threshold [9].
- The 3-day forecast mean is 12.43 µg/L (range 4.79–21.20), with only a 4% chance of exceeding the threshold [11].
- At 5 and 7 days, the mean forecast values are 13.61 µg/L and 14.57 µg/L, with probabilities of exceeding the threshold at 10% and 17%, respectively [12][13]. These probabilities remain low and do not warrant intervention.
- The operational decision guardrail specifies that algaecide addition is only considered when chlorophyll-a exceeds 20 µg/L at the relevant depth, and no toxin-forming bloom is present [1][3].
- There is no evidence of a toxin-forming bloom or toxin risk in the current data.

**Confidence:**  
Confidence in this assessment is high: sensor data are current (0 days old), and the forecast ensemble is robust. However, forecast skill at 7 days is historically weaker than the seasonal climatology, so longer-range projections should be interpreted with caution [2]. This does not affect the current low-risk verdict.

Discussion

Generating forecasts that show the 16-day outcome of 2 di ff erent management choices -activating or deactivating the oxygenation system -is a powerful approach for assisting managers in their decision-making. Managers are given the tools to ' see ' the direct e ff ects of implementing their decision on the future water quality of the reservoir. To the best of our knowledge, other freshwater forecasting systems (e.g., Page et al. 2018, Baracchini et al. 2020) provide future information on lake or reservoir variables but still require managers to determine how their decision-making may interact with forecasted conditions to a ff ect future water quality. While the HOx system forecasts are speci fi c to FCR, we envision that many other management interventions (e.g., algaecide addition, manipulation of in fl ows/out fl ows, extraction of water at di ff erent depths, epilimnetic mixing) could be implemented in forecasting frameworks to examine their potential consequences on water quality.

3. Results

3.1. Chlorophyll-a Variability at FCR and BVR

Seasonal and temporal analyses of Chl-a concentrations revealed greater variability and bloom intensity in FCR than in BVR (Figure 3). Monthly boxplots (Figure 3 a) show clear seasonal patterns at both sites, with elevated Chl-a levels during summer (June-September) and generally reduced levels in winter (December-February). Unlike BVR, FCR exhibited elevated Chl-a concentrations that persisted through late autumn and early winter (November-December). During this period, the median values ranged from 15 to 18 μg/L, with occasional peaks reaching up to 60 μg/L, indicating winter bloom events. In contrast, BVR maintained relatively low Chl-a levels in winter, typically ≤ 10 μg/L. During warmer periods (June-September), peak median values reached ∼ 18 μg/L at FCRand ∼ 15 μg/L at BVR. FCR exhibited greater variability and a higher frequency of bloom events, with values occasionally exceeding 100 μg/L (Figure 3 b). BVR displayed more consistent, moderate Chl-a variability, typically ranging between 5 and 30 μg/L, with the highest Chl-a values of ∼ 33 μg/L. These results highlight pronounced seasonal bloom dynamics and greater interannual bloom frequency and intensity in FCR relative to BVR, suggesting site-specific drivers.

The studies on Beaverdam Reservoir (BVR) and Falling Creek Reservoir (FCR) reveal that temporal variability in biogeochemical variables such as nutrients and chlorophyll-a often exceeds spatial variability, challenging traditional reservoir continuum models. Both reservoirs generally act as sinks for nitrate and total phosphorus but sources for total nitrogen, dissolved organic carbon, and chlorophyll-a, with biogeochemical hotspots most consistently found at the stream-reservoir interface. Hydrological changes and reservoir management significantly influence nutrient dynamics and the spatial distribution of processing hotspots.

Seasonal and physicochemical drivers of chlorophyll-a variability were analyzed in Beaverdam (BVR) and Falling Creek (FCR) Reservoirs, revealing that dissolved organic matter (DOM), day of year (DOY) harmonic, and water temperature are key predictors. SHAP and partial dependence analyses showed that while both reservoirs share dominant drivers, site-specific factors like deep dissolved oxygen (DO) in FCR and Schmidt stability in BVR influence phytoplankton dynamics differently. Temperature and stratification interact to govern nutrient distribution and phytoplankton responses, with FCR exhibiting threshold-like summer blooms linked to warm, stratified conditions, highlighting complex nonlinear ecological responses.

Observed chl a patterns during study period

Chl a exhibited substantial variability over the forecast period, which included two blooms in July 2019 and March -April 2020 and rapid declines due to two copper sulfate dosing events in February and March 2019 (Appendix S 1: Figure S 4). Observed chl a over the forecast period exhibited a median chl a concentration of 7.3  7.2 μ g/L (mean  SD), and a maximum concentration of 55.7 μ g/L, which occurred during the July 2019 bloom. The magnitude of this large bloom greatly exceeded any previous surface bloom recorded by chl a sensors in the reservoir (Appendix S 1: Figure S 4). For comparison, the training data set from May to October of 2013 -2016 had a slightly lower median concentration of 4.9  4.3 μ g/L, and the highest recorded bloom during this period was 24.2 μ g/L in October 2014 (Appendix S 1: Figure S 4). Further, the two blooms that occurred during the forecast period exhibited different patterns. The 2019 bloom lasted from 17 July to 5 August 2019, whereas the 2020 bloom lasted intermittently from 16 March to 23 April 2020 and was much more variable in concentration (Appendix S 1: Figure S 4).

The reservoir was actively managed as a drinking water supply during the forecast period and was treated with copper sulfate twice in 2019 to reduce phytoplankton concentrations. Managers added 200 lbs (90.7 kg) of copper sulfate on 28 February 2019 and 100 lbs (45.4 kg) on 20 March 2019, effectively decreasing chl a concentrations to  0 μ g/L on both days. These time periods were excluded from subsequent analyses because they are not an ecological phenomenon instantiated in the model and thus could not have been predicted.

2.4. Calibration and Analysis Approach

2.4.1. State Variable Observations

Temperature and dissolved oxygen depth profiles were recorded in FCR from 2013 to 2021 at the reservoir's deepest site and were retrieved from the Environmental Data Initiative Repository (Carey, Lewis, et al., 2022). In short, temperature and dissolved oxygen depth profiles were collected with a CTD (Conductivity, Temperature, and Depth) profiler fitted with a SBE 43 Dissolved Oxygen sensor. In addition, discrete depth profiles of temperature and dissolved oxygen were also collected with YSI water quality probes at approximately 1-m intervals (Carey, Wander, et al., 2022). Samples were collected at the deepest site of FCR (near the dam), and other inreservoir transects approximately monthly from October to February, fortnightly from March to May, and weekly from June to September. The YSI temperature profiles complement and fill in for missing CTD data. The observed temperature and dissolved oxygen profile data were spatially interpolated among depths on the data collection days to fill in for missing data and to achieve higher spatial resolution for the calculation of system metrics. Data manipulation, analysis, visualization and computations were undertaken in R (version: 4.1.2).

Throughout the monitoring period, we collected depth profiles of physical, chemical, and biological variables one to three times per week at the deepest sites in FCR and BVR (Figure 1). Profiles were obtained immediately before mixing (before 10:00 on the day the mixer was activated), immediately after mixing (at 18:00 on 30 May for EM 1 and at 13:00 on 28 Jun for EM 2), 24 h post-mixing, and 48-72 h post-mixing in FCR. In BVR, profiles were obtained 24 h before mixing in FCR, 24 h after mixing in FCR, and 48-72 h post-mixing in FCR. We used a 4-Hertz Conductivity, Temperature, and Depth (CTD) profiler (Sea Bird Electronics, Bellevue, WA, USA) equipped with a turbidity sensor (WET Labs ECO fluorometer, Sea Bird Scientific, Bellevue, WA, USA) to collect high-resolution (~1 cm) profiles of temperature and turbidity [27]. Profiles at 1-m resolution of photosyn thetically active radiation (PAR) were collected with an LI-250 underwater light meter (LI-COR, Lincoln, NV, USA) [28]. We also collected depth profiles of total nitrogen (TN), total phosphorus (TP), nitrate (NO 3 -), ammonium (NH 4 + ), and soluble reactive phosphorus (SRP) concentrations using a 4-L van Dorn sampler (Wildco, Yulee, FL, USA) at the depths of the outflow valves of FCR (0.1, 1.6, 3.8, 5, 6.2, 8, and 9 m) and evenly spaced on the vertical profile of BVR (0.1, 3, 6, 9, and 11 m) [29]. Dissolved samples for NO 3 -, NH 4 + , and SRP analysis were filtered through Whatman GF/F filters immediately after collection, and both dissolved and total samples were frozen until analysis. Finally, we collected CTD and Fluoro Probe profiles once a week at four sites in FCR upstream of the deepest site in the riverine zone of the reservoir (Figure 1).
